utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I can see everybody is in his seat. Good morning to the interpreters. Good morning to the Prosecution and to the Defence, to the accused. We can resume. I think today is an important day for the representatives of the American community. There is a holiday today, and I understand why Mr. Hayman didn't want to work this afternoon - now I understand - for Thanksgiving.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. No, Mr. President. Please. We will be working this afternoon, simply not here in the courtroom, I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I'm sure of that. No, just joking. Just joking. Of course, I know we're going to be working this morning only because of the fact that a witness has not arrived, there were airport problems, and there were airport problems all through Europe. All right. We can resume our work with the continuation of the redirect by Mr. Nobilo and the Defence witness, Mr. Katava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: And here he is coming into the courtroom now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I'm going to be very brief because it is a continuation of yesterday's questioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Katava, may we have Defence Exhibit 450? Would you turn to section B, please? In section B, as you know, some cases are mentioned where the victims were Croats, and I would like to draw your attention to document number 19 in particular. From this document, we can see that "Unknown perpetrators" -- and I'm reading the second section -- on the 2nd of August, 1993, around 2.30, came in front of the house of Ivcan Bilic and shot from firearms at the glass cafe entitled Janje. May we have the ELMO on, please? Thank you. This will help our interpreters. So unknown perpetrators arrived at the house of Ivcan Bilic and the Janje cafe and the Janje butcher shop owned by Jozo Marjanovic and Ivcan Bilic respectively and they opened fire at the glass surfaces of these two premises. Tell me, please, the owners of these cafes and shops, were they Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, they were Croats from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you find the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, because this document refers to unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us now move on to document number 20. Document 20, on the 4th of June, '93, you went to the house of Ivica Susanj because unknown perpetrators or a group of perpetrators arrived at the store and fired a burst, damaging all in the glass surfaces in the store, the facade, et cetera, 30 casings, cartridges, were found, and there was general shooting at the premises. Tell me, Frano Susanj from Busovaca, is he a Croat?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Frano Susanj is a Croat from Busovaca. I know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you find the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Once again, this was an official note relating to unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next document is document number 21, and there, in a shop owned by Dragan Lastro, consumer goods shop, a hand bomb was thrown into the shop and it exploded and caused a great deal of damage. The same question: Is Dragan Lastro a Croat?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he is a Croat from the village of Ravan of the Busovaca municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you find the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they were unknown perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let's now move on to document number 22. Document number 22, we have, once again, an official note, first of all your own, where you state that on the 4th of June, 1993, an explosive device was planted in a kiosk owned by Ivica Kristo, nicknamed Taraba, and that one and a half kilos of explosive, Vitezit, was planted, and that four neighbouring kiosks were destroyed in this explosion, which means five kiosks in total from this explosion were destroyed. Tell me, is Taraba a Croat, and were the owners of the neighbouring kiosks, shops, also Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Taraba is a Croat from Busovaca, and the neighbouring premises also belonged to Croats. Some of them were socially owned and some were Muslim owned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, Vitezit, is that an explosive? It is called Vitezit. Is it an explosive manufactured in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it is a type of explosive, and it's called Vitezit, and it is produced in Vitez, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that explosive accessible to many people in view of the fact that it was produced in the region?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I don't want to go through all the documents where the properties of Croats were damaged, but can you tell us, tell the Trial Chamber, in your assessment and judging by logics, who suffered more from crimes, the Croats or Muslims in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the Croats were more numerous victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Because there were more Croats living there and more Croat-owned property.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And another question that was mentioned yesterday: Do you still maintain that crime had its criminal logics and not a nationalistic logic?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I maintain that criminality and the crime rate followed its own logics and had nothing to do with nationality or ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now a final document and a final set of questions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D451, D451A for the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you take a look at the original document, please, and the file number, part of the document has been typewritten on a typewriter, and there is a line and the year, and after that, by hand, the file number has been entered by hand. Can you tell us the situations when this was done?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, this was done when we did not know the file number to come, when the administrative secretary was unavailable, so we just left a space for it to be introduced later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And then you would write it in in handwriting, by hand?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I would now like to draw your attention to this particular document. You told the Trial Chamber that you questioned people entering Busovaca, as well Croats, that you questioned them in the same way that you questioned Muslims wishing to depart from Busovaca, and I would now like to read parts of the document and then ask you questions. It is a document from the police station of Busovaca where Ivanka Zrnic and Zeljko Zrnic make their statements. Tell us, please, are they Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they are Croats from Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So I'm going to read some sections from this text. "On 18 April 1993, I (Ivanka Zrnic) was in the house with my family. I was awakened by loud shooting, and we all took shelter on the ground floor of the house at my mother-in-law's. There were my husband, two children, mother-in-law, uncle, aunt, cousin, his wife and three little girls." And I'm going to skip a few lines and continue. Apart from us in the neighbourhood, there were two elderly men who were killed later on, Ivan Vidovic, born in 1904, and Anto Vidovic, born in 1906. "Ivan was taken out and shot, and then they set fire to his house. Anto was killed in the house. We were lying on the floor when a Muslim soldier from the 7th Muslim Brigade approached the window and, without a word, fired a whole clip from an automatic rifle at us. On this occasion, my daughter Magdalena, three-and-a-half years old, was hit and she died almost immediately. She was hit in the right cheek and the bullet went out through the back on her head. I was also wounded in the head then. The person who did this was a man nicknamed Hodja from the village of Puhovac, Zenica municipality, but I don't know his full name." She describes him and says he looked like a Muslim from the 7th Muslim Brigade. For her husband, she said that three men made him lie down on the ground. "My husband had come out with our dead girl in his arms and he lay down with her. He asked if he can put the child to the side, but the Hodja just kicked him in the head with his boot and said: 'Lie down, you Ustasha mother fucker.'" And then it goes on to describe the tortures suffered in the Muslim gaol, and it goes on to say: When they arrived there, "a man started questioning us," quite obviously your colleague, a policeman. He asked me what had happened, "but when I started telling him, he interrupted me and did not allow me to talk." I'm going to ask you whether you recognise this document and do you know Josip Grubesic and do you recognise the signature, that is, the man taking the statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Josip Grubesic is my colleague from the police station at Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you recall this particular event when you took this statement?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I recall this event. There were great casualties, and I remember Ivanka Zrnic well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did incidents of this kind compel people to flee from Zenica towards Busovaca, I mean Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. For reasons of this kind, the Croats from Zenica fled to Busovaca and further afield as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did it frequently happen that these same Croats who were the victims in one area, on one territory, very often came as displaced persons and committed crimes where they came?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we had refugees who were desperate and who wanted to get their own on others and we had a lot of problems with people of this kind because of the situation they found themselves in because they had been left without anything and had suffered great torture and hardships.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this the reason that it was so difficult to control the situation and to find the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is, among others, one of the reasons for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have completed this document, and we tender this document along with the others we brought up yesterday in evidence. I'm going to give you the exact numbers in just a moment. They are D413, A and B, D443, D444, D445, D446, D447, and D448 as well as D449, D450, and D451. We tender these into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nobilo. No objections from the Prosecution? Mr. Cayley?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President, apart from the reservation of our position on tab H in Exhibit 450 which we've discussed already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Riad, do you have any questions to ask the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen, do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. You were talking about your passport. Could you tell us: When was the passport issued?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: My passport was issued in 1995, in the consulate in Mostar, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did you have a passport before?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, never. I never had a former passport or a currently valid passport.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How were you described in this passport? Were you described as a Croatian citizen or as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm a citizen of Bosnia and Herzegovina but also a citizen of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: How were you described in the passport?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the passport, it says Slavko Katava, born on the 21st of September, 1956, in Donje Polje, the municipality of Busovaca, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I got this passport in the consulate in Mostar, the consulate of the Republic of Croatia, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: The passport contains no reference to your citizenship, does it?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: In order to have this passport, I have to have Croatian citizenship, and I do have dual citizenship.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now let us turn to these declarations or statements in this big red file. When somebody came to you at the station and made a statement and the statement was recorded by you or one of your colleagues, how many copies of the statement were made?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honours, we usually took these statements and made three or four copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, what would you do with them, the three or four copies?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: We would open a file. We would open a file, Your Honour, and we would leave it for further usage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you send any of the copies to any other authority, the Prosecutor's Office, say?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you have seen these copies in the file. Could you tell the Trial Chamber where these copies were made, what document they were made from? Were they made from a copy in the possession of your police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, these documents were copies of the original documents that we made in the police station, but where these copies were made, that, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, we have a declaration made by a gentleman by the name of Fikret Zulum. You saw that declaration?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, would I be right in saying that there was no great urgency about the contents of that declaration?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't really understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Very well. I shall pass the question. Could that document have waited until the morning when the administrative secretary returned to the office so that you might get from her a protocol number and insert it in the blank space?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: One couldn't really wait there. I know Mr. Fikret Zulum personally. He's a former policeman, and he reported of his own free will because he didn't want to have any problems. He came to the station and sought appropriate protection. He said, "I'm here. My wife and my children have left. I don't want to have any problems." He spoke in that sense, and then a colleague of his, a policeman, took a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, some of the statements which you took were taken by you after the administrative secretary left for the day. Could some of those statements have waited until she returned in the morning?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some could, some that were not urgent, or if the party concerned could come later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, you served for a number of years in this police station.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Did your police station adopt a procedure for identifying the appropriate protocol number for a document when the administrative secretary was not there?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Suppose she was ill for a day or two or three, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Then the head of the police station would appoint a replacement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Suppose there was no replacement for a day, what would happen?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, nothing. We'd write documents without a protocol number, and these documents would wait for a protocol number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, look at Mr. Zulum's statement again. It is document 36. I am looking at the English version. Would you, sir, say that Mr. Zulum is not there reporting the commission of any specific crime?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And that he is also not seeking any permit from the police station whether to stay in Busovaca or to leave Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What he is doing, in effect, is this: That he was blaming the Muslim side for the outbreak of any conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, he panicked, Your Honour. He is a neighbour of the police station and a former policeman, and he knew all of us, and he came to tell us that he was frightened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Are there any other statements in this file from Muslims which also blame the Muslim side for the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, do you agree that all the statements in or under tab F in the file are statements made by Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you also agree that those statements have blank spaces in the serial number section?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, look at section G in the file. Is my impression correct that the statements in that section are statements made by Croats?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is my impression also correct that all of those statements have completed serial numbers?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but these statements were taken by my colleague, Josip Grubesic, who worked with the secretary. He would only do the first shift, so he always had the protocol handy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, while you have that big file before you, would you look at document 96? Now, this document is signed by the head of the municipality, Niko Grubesic. Was that something like the mayor or so? What is the closest I.D. which corresponds to that, the mayor?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, mayor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you look at the subject heading at the top "Re: Proposal for the First Stage of the Return of Refugees and Persons Expelled from the Territory of Busovaca Municipality with Indications of the Future Stages of Return." Would you say that the impression given out is that the head of the municipality was talking of all displaced persons and of proposals for resettling all of them?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, look just before the columned area. You see a capital A, "Displaced Persons and Refugees of Croatian Nationality." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Is there, Mr. Katava, a B section? We have an A section here. Is there a B section somewhere?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, section B, "Muslim and Other Refugees," was provided by the deputy president of the municipality, a Muslim. He made this same kind of document, and these documents were sent to humanitarian organisations and other organisations dealing with the resettlement of refugees.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Perhaps I wasn't clear. The reader reading this document sees on page 1 a heading beginning with capital A. I am asking you whether, later on in this document, there is a heading beginning capital B.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: No. Now, look at page 1. You have a number 2 which says that "In 1991, Bosniaks living in Busovaca numbered 8.484 or 44.9 per cent." Do you see that line?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, is my recollection correct that you told us that 90 per cent of the Muslim population in Busovaca left Busovaca? Is my impression correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you heard it right, but only from the town of Busovaca, not from the territory of the entire municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Well, what would 90 per cent of 8.484 be? Would it be something like 7.200 or how many persons would you say left the municipality of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not say that they left from the entire territory of Busovaca but only from the town of Busovaca. So 90 per cent relates to the urban population of Busovaca, not people from the rural areas, they didn't leave. So I wasn't talking about these 8.484, but I was talking about the people from town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That is why I inserted an alternative in my question and asked you, how many do you say left? You were a senior police officer, and you were concerned with the goings and comings of people. People going had to get a permit from you.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Over a thousand people left from town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Do you agree that no where in this document is reference made to the fact that over 1.000 Muslims left the city of Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, I gathered from you that your understanding of the situation was that the Muslim sector of the population of Busovaca accepted the takeover of power by the HVO. Is my understanding of your evidence correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some did not accept this fact, and that is why they left, while others remained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I see. Let's talk about the Muslim police chief who moved to Kacuni and who took his men with him there. By doing so, he effectively gave up territory which he controlled as a police officer; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. He left from the police station and went to Kacuni, which is a territory with a Muslim majority population, but all of this is within the territory of the municipality of Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: And he left just after the takeover of power by the HVO; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, at that time, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you relate the takeover of power by the HVO to the fact that he left for Kacuni?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: That is possible too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have only one question. It has to do with the idea of protection for Muslims. You said to us several times, in answer to questions that were asked, that this system for giving authorisations for leaving and coming into Busovaca was to protect the Muslims, to ensure law and order, and to protect them. But to protect them from what, from attacks by the Croats; is that what you meant?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: From attacks by criminals, individuals, criminal groups, persons who wanted to take revenge too who could have mistreated them and persecuted them. We asked them to tell us whether somebody was mistreating them so that we could resolve the problem in that case and that we could help them stay in their homes in this way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, you would ask them that, but would they always answer that they were being threatened? Did they say that they were being threatened?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: In cases where they were threatened, we intervened, and we helped these people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, that's not quite what I asked. First of all, they said to you that they were threatened. Did they specify what type of threat they were under because there's no trace of that in the statements or at least very rarely?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: In certain cases, it was so. People came and said that they were threatened by individuals who said that they did not belong there and that they would kill them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Then, as you, yourself, said, they were only isolated cases.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Let me ask you my two questions. There were the isolated cases when someone would say, "I'm coming to the police station, I am Muslim, because my Croatian neighbours or others want my house." There were not very many of those cases; is that right? Is that what you're saying? They were isolated cases. That's what you said.

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I meant that this was done by individuals, but there were quite a few such cases, especially refugees coming from other areas. They sought accommodation, and we intervened in such cases, but, at any rate, we didn't allow anyone to be kicked out of his own house or his own apartment. We would not allow this kind of thing to happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: But that has to do with the isolated cases. There were individual cases where the threats were individual threats, but most of them were not individualised threats, and that is why that system for authorising entrance and exit to the city was put into place. Now, was that system something that the population experienced in a rather positive way, that is, the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, yes, it was in the interest of all to know who was going where and who was doing what. For safety reasons, it was in the interest of their security.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: How many people did you have working in your police station?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Some of us worked at the station, and some were at the frontline. They were involved in defence. So there were about 20 of us at the station and 30, approximately, at the frontline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: As regards that system, about how many people would come every day to register, to be allowed to either come in or to go out of the territory? Each day, about how many people would come in?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it depends. Two or three persons, perhaps one person would go and two or three would come, something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So you would intervene when the threat was specific. Did you have any problems with the Croatian people that you would intervene on behalf of?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we had major problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Therefore, the Croatian part of the population didn't always like what you were doing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was very difficult with them. They were saying, "You are our own policemen. Why are you persecuting us?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So that, in the end, this authorising system must have been very constraining for the Muslims, not very effective, because you didn't have a lot of men working for you at your police station, and the Croatian population didn't have a very high opinion of you. Would you agree with me if I were to say that the system was somewhat absurd?

utterances.speaker: SLAVKO KATAVA (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know if it was absurd or not, but that is the way it functioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Katava, the Tribunal thanks you for having come to The Hague to testify in this trial. The usher will now escort you out of the courtroom, and we will continue our work.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you too, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think that the next witness is covered by protective measures, and in order to set up the courtroom, we are going to take a 15-minute or 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Resume the hearing now. Have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, will you be doing the direct examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is a protected witness that we have next. He would also like to be given a pseudonym and face distortion. We would like to have a private session at one point because some of the facts might help to identify him, so we would like to move into a private session at some point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I thought this was a closed session. Is it not a closed session? This is a public session? Oh, it's simply putting in protective measures. If it is a witness whose name we're not going to say, therefore his pseudonym is what?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be Witness DM, "M" like "Mary."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Let's have the witness brought in, Witness DM.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Do you hear me, Witness DM?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First we're going to ask you to verify your name on this piece of paper but without your saying it. Be sure that this is, in fact, you. Is that correct? Don't say your name.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (Nods in the affirmative)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing for a few moments, as long as it takes to take your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated now. You are covered by protective measures. You will be called Witness DM and your face cannot be seen. In respect of everything else, this is a public hearing, but at any point, the attorneys, especially the Defence attorneys who called you, can ask for a completely closed session if there is no objection by the opposing party, and we do that for your benefit. Do not be afraid of anything. You are before Judges. You can speak without fear, and you will see that everything will go along smoothly. Mr. Nobilo, don't hesitate to ask for a closed session whenever you like. Proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Witness DM, you are retired; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before we go on with the examination-in-chief, we are going to hand round a map to explain to the Trial Chamber where you lived up until the conflict broke out between the Muslims and the Croats in the Vitez municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This is the original map and a legend.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D452 and D452A for the legend. I don't know whether the document is confidential or not. If you would let me know, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Witness DM, could you take up the pointer -- I think you will find it on the table in front of you -- and show us on the map that is located on your left-hand side the village where you lived up until the conflict. You can use your glasses, if necessary. But don't move it, please, because we won't be able to see it. Don't move the map. Leave the map as it stands, please. Can you indicate the village of Poculica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: This is it here (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that is the village you lived in prior to the conflicts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Trial Chamber, please, the local community, the municipality, the local community and the self-governing community, which villages did it incorporate at that time? It did not incorporate Poculica alone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Your Honours, the village -- the local community of Poculica encompassed Poculica with a gravitation towards the road running from Vitez to Zenica. On the right-hand side lies the village of Prnjavor, and further on, one and a half to two kilometres, you have the village of Vrhovine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Does that mean that this local community, as you call it, is composed of the villages of Poculica, Prnjavor, and Vrhovine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, please, if you can, the composition of the inhabitants? How many Muslims and how many Croats lived in the village of Poculica and how many in the local community that you described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Your Honours, the local community of Poculica, the Croats lived along the road. Up until half the village, from the direction of Vitez, these are Croat houses. Towards Vjetrenice is the mixed population. To the right of the village of Poculica lies the village of Prnjavor which is a purely Muslim village. Further to the right of Prnjavor, one and a half to two kilometres, we have the village of Vrhovine, which is once again a purely Muslim village. They are fairly large villages. I don't know the exact number of inhabitants, but there are about 70 Croat houses, approximately, and Muslims in those three villages, I would say there were about 250.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Muslim houses, you mean?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell the Court, please, in the municipality of Vitez, how many family members are there to one house or household? What is the average?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, some people had five or six, some households numbered two or three, some numbered seven or eight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. The conflict between the Muslims and Croats in the Vitez municipality began on the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court, before the actual conflict on the 16th of April took place, did you notice anything that would indicate that a conflict was imminent? Did you notice anything, any strange goings-on, or was everything as it was usually?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Before the Croat and Muslim conflict, the Muslims had patrols above the village at Vjetrenice and they were called Gajevi. On the lower part of the village from the Vitez direction at Stipica, they had some bunkers, trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And the situation, what was that like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, it was tolerable. There were no major problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of people, foreign Muslims, some Mujahedins, coming to your local community, people who had never lived there, that is to say, prior to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: This was rumoured, yes, it was rumoured that they existed, but when, on the 16th of April, I sat in my house with my wife, at about 9.00, in my yard, there was shooting from an automatic rifle. When the shooting stopped, my wife went out to see what was going on, and they said, "Who's in the house?" They asked her, "Who's in the house?" And she said, "My husband." And I went out, and they sent us to the village of Prnjavor, they expelled us to the village of Prnjavor, to a youth centre, all the men, and everybody that did not escape was rounded up and taken to the prison at the youth centre in Prnjavor. The men went to the youth centre and the women were taken to the basements of two or three Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who rounded up the men and the women and what nationality were those individuals who were taken to the prisons, both men and women, and which ethnic group did the people who rounded them up belong to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Those of us who were taken to prison were all Croats, both men, women, and children, and we were taken by soldiers of the army -- the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, the men and women that were rounded up, were there HVO soldiers amongst you, that is to say, men wearing uniform and carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: No, none of us had weapons. Some of us, two or three, did have uniforms on. It was a reserve formation. And some of us went up towards Travnik to Slatke Vode, which was where the frontlines were together with the Muslims, so the Muslims and Croats were there on the frontlines towards the Serbs, towards Travnik and Lasva.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: All the rest, all the other men and women and children, were they all civilians, Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, they were all Croat civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many men had been rounded up and how many women and children? How many were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I think there were about 30 of us in the youth centre and we were made to lie down on the concrete. There was no protection on the floor. It was just a concrete flooring.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "us," you mean the men, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Men.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What about the women and children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: The women were in the basements. I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What kind of conditions prevailed? You said that there were no beds, that you had to lie down on the concrete floor. Did you have any bathrooms and showers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: No, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have a toilet?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, we could go outside during the day and we had a bucket during the night and we were locked in overnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, you were rounded up and locked up on the 16th of April, 1993, were you not? What time did they take you to Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: It was about 9.00 or 9.30, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you use your pointer and tell us whether number 2 is the location where you were when they arrested you and took you to the centre in Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Poculica is here and these two places are linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you explain to the Court, between the night of the 18th and 19th of April, 1993, the commander of the Military Police came to the prison. What did he want?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: At around the 18th of April, 1993, the chief of the military Muslim police came to the prison and took 20 individuals with him. He gave us guards and they took us down towards the station which was called the Han company in Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you show us Sivrino Selo on the map? Is it located by number 3? Take your pointer, please. Look at number 3, and is that Sivrino Selo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes. Here it is (indicating).

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So that's where you were taken. Now, what happened there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Two of the soldiers were killed, and they told us that we would be a human shield while they buried their dead, and we stood around them as a human shield to prevent anybody shooting at them from the frontlines down below.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "they," do you mean the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And their soldiers were burying their own dead; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you Croat civilians who had been taken prisoner had to stand around them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes. We were a human shield.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did they say to stop your own people from shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were you standing around in a semicircle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes. Not a full circle but two-thirds of a circle, looking from the bottom up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In that way, did you protect the people doing the digging from the HVO positions with your bodies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, with our bodies we protected them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you have to stand the whole time or were you allowed to sit down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: While they were digging the graves, we had to stand. Then we went up to the village which was further up ahead, and we waited until dusk and then they brought them and buried them and then we were returned at night to the prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one moment, please. While the digging was going on, while the graves were being dug, you civilians had to remain standing; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In order to protect them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now move on to the following day when the chief of the Military Police came to the prison once again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, the same chief of Military Police came once again, and he selected 18 men and took them down below where they remained the entire time until the exchange took place. I remained in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Where did they take them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: To Sivrino Selo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So they had to work for the frontline. So it was at the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, at the BH army frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were these stronger, youngish men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, he left me as an elderly one and a few others, but they took some younger ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You remained in prison, and sometime around the 23rd of April, 1993, a tragic event occurred in prison. Could you explain to the Court what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: We were locked up during the night. There was a lock on the door, and the guard was outdoors, and we were relieving ourselves inside. At daybreak, we heard a male voice shouting, the guard, saying, "Open up." And the guard said, "I can't. I don't have the key." And the other one was screaming out loud and saying, "Open up." And he said, "I can't. The key is at the command." So then he shot through the door. People started screaming inside, there were ten of us, there were ten men there, and they also brought in five women to wait for exchange in Preocica, and I think he shot an entire clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How many bullets is that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: A clip? I don't know. Thirty-six, I think, 36 are in a clip. And when he stopped shooting, the door opened and the room was full of smoke. The balance was nine wounded, three killed, and three were intact but in a state of great shock. I haven't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Please go on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: A few minutes later, nurses came -- or, rather, orderlies came and carried the wounded to Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You remained intact; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: The three of us remained alive and three were killed. Two officers came and they wrote down the names of the dead and they took photographs of them, and when they finished that, one of them said, "Why did he do this? Why didn't he throw two grenades? All the pigs would have been dead." And he asked us, "Why are you trembling? Why are you pretending?" And that day, all of us were transferred to a bigger Croat house, both the men and the women, and then they took better care of us, a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The next event that I would like you to tell the Court about was the one from the 28th of April when they came to get you and another friend of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, could we please move into private session for a minute only because this could lead to identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just a minute. We don't want the public to hear this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Go ahead. All right. We are in public session again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, 1993, through the International Red Cross, we were exchanged, and I went to the town of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We are going to stop at this point now and we are going to move to the present time. The Croatian houses in the lower part of the village, closer to Vitez, this is a purely Croatian part of the village. In what shape are the houses now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: These houses are completely burned down, destroyed -- well, not totally, not to the ground, but sort of half. I don't know how to put it, but some have been burned down more than a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So they were razed to the ground?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, they were. I mean, that is the part where only Croats live. That is a bit less than half of the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So we're talking about the total number of Croat houses. But tell me, in this mixed area that you live in, have the Croats come back or does somebody live in their houses?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: In our houses, those that remained intact, they were looted. Everything was taken away from them. But there are some people living in them. Our houses were looted, our trees were cut down and orchards too. I was in Vitez. It was terrible. We were surrounded totally. And a lot of our civilians and soldiers were killed, and my son was killed. For one month, he lay dead, and we could not bury him, and it was not only him, there were others. They did not allow us to get them out and bury them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DM.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We have thus concluded the direct examination. Mr. President, we have completed --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Please, I would like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But the rules are that once we have finished, it's finished.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I know, but I have something very important to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Well, if you have something you would like to add, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know that you have many things to say, and you will say them, but for the moment --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I won't take too much of your time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: In 1995, when the fighting ended between the Croats and the Muslims, we went on an official visit to our dead and to the cemeteries. When we came, it was a sight to behold. The fence was taken away, all of it. The chapel was burned down. All the tombstones were broken. After that, some donors gave us assistance, and we put a fence around our dead once again. When we went there again after some time, again, the fence was missing. Again, they took it away. And the relationships are not really very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness DM. You will now be asked some questions by the representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor, and then the Judges may ask you a few questions as well. Mr. Harmon, if you want to ask a few questions, ask Witness DM a few questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness DM.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm Mark Harmon, and I'm from the Prosecutor's Office, and my colleagues, to the right is Mr. Andrew Cayley, and to his right is Mr. Gregory Kehoe. I don't have many questions to ask you this morning, but I want to ask you initially some questions about the village where you lived. I have had an opportunity to take a look at Prosecutor's Exhibit 46, which is a copy of the 1991 census. In the census figures for the village of Poculica, it indicates that there were, in 1991, 739 residents, 408 of whom were of Croatian descent and 321 of whom were of Muslim descent. Is that consistent with what you recall the village population to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes. In the village of Poculica proper, which gravitates towards the road, there were more Croats than Muslims, more Croat houses than Muslim houses. Perhaps I could say, not very precisely, but I think that there were about 70 Croat houses and about 40 Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, in the community itself, you said there was a village called Prnjavor. Does the village of Prnjavor appear separately from the village of Poculica on this particular map or is Prnjavor contained within the area that says "Poculica"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Officially speaking, these three villages are called or referred to as Poculica, but each village has its individual name. Poculica is Poculica; Prnjavor is Prnjavor; Vrhovine is Vrhovine. But as one entity, the local community was the local community of Poculica, using the name of that village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And from testimony that we have heard previously and from, as I understand it, your testimony, the village of Poculica was a village where there was a part of the village that was predominantly Croat, inhabited by the Croats, a part of the village that was predominantly inhabited by Muslims, and a part of the village that was more integrated, was more mixed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Down below the mosque up to the school building and 100 metres below the school, the village was purely Croat. The village is all one, but Croats lived there. Whereas from the school upwards, this was a mixed community.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DM, in that part of the village that was purely Croat, approximately how many houses were there in that part of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, to give you an exact number, perhaps up to 30 houses, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness DM, you lived in the mixed part of the village, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And your neighbours, you had Muslims as neighbours, did you not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, I did. They were Muslims. My neighbours were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, before the Muslim/Croat war started, you got along well with your Muslim neighbours, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, we lived normally, not too much love lost between us, but we lived normally. Well, more or less, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the morning of the 16th of April, you said that what first attracted your attention was the sounds of an automatic rifle being fired at approximately 9.00 in the morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Between 9.00 and 9.30, thereabouts. That was the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you then went outside and were confronted by a Muslim soldier; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: There were three soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: One, I did not know, and two were covered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when the Muslim soldiers wanted to take you to the community centre, didn't your Muslim neighbour, a woman, attempt to intervene and say to those soldiers, "It's okay. He can come and stay at my house." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I remember it well. (redacted) (redacted) said we could stay, we should stay, but the soldiers didn't let us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I've taken care of the matter, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, thereafter, you were taken initially, were you not, to the community centre, but the community centre was locked, wasn't it, and you then were taken to a house belonging to Nasid Bertas; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and that man was very nice towards us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So when you and the other Bosnian Croats from the village of Poculica were taken down to Mr. Bertas's house, in fact, you were offered coffee, and the treatment that was given to you was quite proper, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Bertas was a Muslim, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were you later in the day put into this particular community centre, you and other men?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: That day, I was taken first.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, approximately what time did you arrive at Mr. Bertas's house, at about 9.30 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Between 9.30 and 10.00, thereabouts. The community centre was locked, and one man banged on it with his foot. They took us back to the house, and when they managed to open the door, they took us back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember what time that was, when you were taken into the community centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I didn't have a watch on me, so I can't tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. And then you remained in the community centre, I take it, as a detainee, unless and until you wanted to go outside to relieve yourself, but for all intents and purposes, you remained in the community centre until the events that you've described in your testimony, when you were taken to be used as a human shield, when you were taken to Barin Gaj to retrieve a body; is that fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, that's all true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were at the community centre, did your Muslim neighbours bring food to you and to the other people who were being detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, Muhamed Dzidic brought us food and coffee, and he was very good to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what about Nasid Bektas? He's a Muslim as well. How did he treat you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: With Nasid Bektas, the women were located in his basement and in two or three other basements, and Nasid Bektas was correct in his behaviour towards them. He wouldn't allow any mistreatment of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: -- by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. When you stayed in the community centre, did you have blankets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: We had one blanket. Atif Taunic brought us a blanket.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Atif Taunic, is he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when was the first time you heard shelling from artillery?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: When we were locked up. In a couple of days' time, shooting could be heard. I don't know where it was coming from. We were inside, you see, probably somewhere around the frontline down below, but there was a frontline in several positions. There was an encirclement, and battles were being waged.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Am I correct in saying, Witness DM, that the first artillery impacts that you heard in the village of Poculica occurred after you were detained in the community centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: It could be heard. Whether there was mortar fire or whether it was the artillery, I don't know. I'm not a military expert to be able to assess what type of shooting actually took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And it was the first time you heard that kind of fire, be it mortar or artillery, after you were detained in the community centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there was shooting then, and when I was in Vitez, there was shooting all the time. There were attacks all the time by that army because there were two corps stationed there, the 3rd and 7th Corps, and they had made an encirclement around Vitez, like a belt on a pair of trousers. And even at my age, I had to go up to the frontline and work for the needs of the frontline and the army because there were very few of us, and there was great pressure being exerted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you, Witness DM, were you aware that, on the 16th of April, 1993, HVO artillery positions from Vitez, from the area of Gradina, were shelling the village of Poculica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you another question. You mentioned that there were some but, I take it, very few people who were of Croatian descent, who lived in Poculica, who were in the HVO, and who went to the frontlines to fight against the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many people fell into that category?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: There weren't many of them but they did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, before the events that you've described on the 16th of April took place, were there any Bosnian army units, headquarters, or locations where they conducted their business located in the village of Poculica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: In the village of Prnjavor where Prnjavor starts, about 100 metres in depth, there was a big house there, and that was a fighting unit of some kind, and they said that there was some foreigners there as well, and we could hear them training there. They would say "Allah-u-ekber" and cries of that kind. That could be heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So that appeared to be a Muslim fighting unit of some kind located in the village of Poculica or the community of Poculica, I should say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, that unit was there, yes, but after the Muslims went, they didn't go up to Slatke Vode. They were just there for the needs of that particular village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, how far away was Poculica from the frontline? I'm talking about the frontline between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: There was no frontline at Poculica. The frontline was down below Sivrino Selo, towards Han Kompanja, and at Krizancevo Selo, the side towards Zenica and lower there, Gavrina Kuce. And then on the other side, there is Kruscica, and that was where the other frontline was and up by Bukve, and that went right the way around, an encirclement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question to you, Witness DM, is approximately how far away from Poculica was the closest frontline between the Muslim forces and the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: From Poculica, well, below Poculica, five kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you were rounded up from your home about 9.00 to 9.30 in the morning on the 16th of April. Witness DM, were you aware that at 5.30 in the morning on the 16th of April the HVO attacked the village of Ahmici, the village of Vitez, the village of Donja Veceriska, the village of Santici, and the village of Nadioci? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that, no. I'm a pensioner, and I was at home, and I slept a little late, and I can't tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever hear about the events that occurred at Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, it was rumoured that there were casualties down there, but I don't know who or what.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the village of Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said in your testimony, Witness DM, that you came back to your village, and I believe it was in -- when was that exactly? I don't have a note on that. Was that in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: When we went to visit the cemetery, I think that was in 1995, in the spring of 1995, at the beginning of spring, because the fighting lasted until the winter of 1994, so we didn't go that year, but we went in 1995. I think that was when it was, and this was an official visit, a group visit, and we were escorted by the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you testified that the homes in the purely Croat areas were burned to the ground or destroyed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, they can't be used for living in. Some were more destroyed; others were less destroyed, less damaged. They weren't all burnt to the ground, but they were destroyed, so they would have to be repaired.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Witness DM, did you see any of those houses actually being destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: That's a superfluous question. I said that there were no roofs, there were no upper stories, upper floors, and so the houses are uninhabitable. They have been destroyed. Of course, not totally, not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think, Witness DM, you misunderstood my question. I clearly understand the state of those houses and their condition when you saw them in 1995. My question to you was: Did you see them actually being destroyed by somebody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Oh, no, no, I didn't see that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, while you were in Vitez, while you lived in Vitez, were you aware that the HVO continued to shell Poculica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I don't know that. I did some work for some time and was in the work platoon, but who was shooting, I don't know that. A mortar fell three metres from where I was, but I was not killed myself. And one day, a grenade fell from Bukve or I don't know from where, and it killed eight children on the spot, eight children who were playing in the yard. Eight children were dead on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DM, when you went back to the village of Poculica, did you tour the area of the village that was mostly Muslim?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: When we went to the cemetery, we passed by the road, but I did not go into the houses and move around the houses. I didn't move around that area, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you determine whether any of those houses had been damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Which houses?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The houses that were in the predominantly Muslim section of the village of Poculica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: The Muslim part of the village of Poculica, no, the houses were not destroyed there. One house was destroyed up there by the school, one house, and several sheds near the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What about in the area that was the part of the village where you lived, the mixed area, where there were Croats living amongst Muslims? What was the condition of that part of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, in that part of the village, there are about ten houses. One shed was burnt down, along with a cow in it, and another across the road, another barn was burnt down there, and I don't remember anything else being burnt in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, was the part of the village that was exclusively Croat, where the 30 houses had been destroyed, was that the part of the village of Poculica that was closest to Vitez, closest to the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, where the village begins, it is by the village of Dubravica. There's Dubravica, and then you have Poculica. It's the lower half, and that's where the Croats were, and that's what was burnt down.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DM, you were exchanged on the 1st of May, 1993. To your knowledge, did any Croats from the village of Poculica remain in the village after you were exchanged, and did they remain in the village throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, two or three families remained one day, and then the next day they had to leave immediately, under pressure, that's what they said, and nobody remained after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to turn your attention very briefly to the unfortunate and sad events that you described when a soldier came to the community centre and fired into the building itself. I'd like to focus your attention on that. Approximately what time of the day did that occur? Was that in the morning or the afternoon or the evening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: The morning before 9.00, probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: From what you describe, the soldier -- could you see the soldier who did the shooting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: You cannot see through a door.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So you could only hear him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I heard a voice shouting "Open up," but I don't know the voice. I don't know who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did there appear to be an argument between the guard who was guarding you and the other people who were in the community centre and the soldier who did the firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he was shouting, "I don't have a key," and the attacker said, "Open up," and the other one said, "The key is at the command," and the command was 10 or 15 metres away from us at the most, and he did not wait for the key. He shot through the door. The door was in the middle of the room, and it was a metal door.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DM, in listening to this argument between the person who shot and the guard, did he say anything else that gave you any indication of why he shot into the room where you and your friends were being detained? As you look back on it now, is there anything that he said that suggests to you a reason or a motive why he did that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: They say that a relative of his was killed at that line and that he wanted to take revenge for him by killing us. That was the assumption, and that was the rumour, and I cannot confirm it 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn very briefly to another area, and that deals with the occasion when you described --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm trying to decide whether or not this, Mr. President, was in private session, if you would just give me a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me come back to the time very quickly, Mr. DM, after the events when your companions were shot and wounded. You said that medical help arrived. Did it arrive fairly quickly after the event itself, and were your companions taken to the hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: A medical team arrived after 10 or 15 minutes approximately, and they were taken to the hospital in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, the occasion when you were used as a human shield to allow the Muslim soldiers to bury their dead, that was clearly wrong, wasn't it? That conduct was wrong, wasn't it? Civilians shouldn't have been used as human shields; isn't that your opinion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, that's the way it was. It shouldn't have been that way. Because they wanted to be safe and they didn't want to be shot at, they used us as a shield to protect themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you ever hear of the HVO ever doing similar types of things to civilians, to Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: That, I do not know. I didn't walk around with them so that I could say so. It's the soldiers who were in the army who know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Witness DM, I have finished my examination. Thank you very much. Mr. President, I have concluded my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, do you want to add anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very, very briefly. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just two or three more questions. We don't want to keep you much longer. When were you born? Could you please remind us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: On the 1st of January, 1926.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When the Prosecutor was questioning you, when you were on the Croatian side, you said that although you were born in 1926, that you were digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's what I said. I was digging trenches for the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, did you belong to a work platoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I shouldn't have been. I wasn't supposed to be. But due to the circumstances, I tried to help the defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did all the men in Vitez belong to the army or did they help the army by digging trenches, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, older people who were over 60, they were not soldiers. They were there as manpower.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you were digging, was this at the frontline, at the frontline?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Well, of course it was. Of course. At the fighting line. That's where you dig trenches. Because many times, the line would fall, and then you'd have to dig another one, and then the soldiers wouldn't have enough time to do so and then the civilians would have to help them due to circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. And now another area. You said that before the conflict, in Prnjavor, there was a unit of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and that there were foreigners among them. What did people say? What did these foreigners look like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: I didn't see them, but people say that there were some foreigners there, and the one who came into my yard, he was a stranger to me and he had a different way of talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you could hear these units shouting "Allah-u-ekber"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. They were exercising, they were doing something.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And you said that they did not go to Slatke Vode, so this unit was not engaged in warfare?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: No, no, no. They went together, the Muslims and the Croats, and my late son also went there when it was his turn to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And this fighting unit consisting of strangers who were outside the area of your village and who were shouting "Allah-u-ekber" and who did not go to fight against the Serbs -- what about the Croats? Were you afraid of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: There were not only strangers there, not only foreigners, there were locals and foreigners, strangers, so, oh, it wasn't that easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us move further on. You mentioned to the Prosecutor that in the mixed part of the village that a cow and a barn had burned down and yet another shed, and who were the owners of these sheds and barns and cows that had burned down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: One was owned by Ante Jurcevic and the other one, it was owned by Bozo Kristo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What are they by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see any Muslim houses or barns or sheds on fire in that mixed part of the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS DM
utterances.text: There wasn't anyone to torch it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The Croatian part of the village was destroyed, and it is five kilometres away from the frontline, as you said. Tell the Court, what do you think?
